title: Why law firms miss prospective client calls, and fixes for Mac teams in 2026
metaTitle: Law firms miss prospective client calls: costs, causes and fixes
description: Only 40% of law firms answered a prospect's call in a 2024 secret-shopper study. Here is what it costs, why it happens and fixes you can use.
targetKeyword: law firms miss prospective client calls
intro: Many law firms miss prospective client calls, and the rate has been falling. In a 2024 secret-shopper study of 500 US firms, only 40% answered a prospect's call, down from 56% in 2019. This page covers what missed calls cost, why they happen, and fixes you can start today on a Mac without buying anything.
tldr: In a 2024 secret-shopper study of 500 US firms, 40% answered a prospect's call, down from 56% in 2019.
No peer-reviewed study measures how much revenue missed calls cost. Treat vendor dollar figures with care.
The usual causes are no owner for intake, voicemail with no reason to wait, and screening that hides new numbers.
Start with a two-week call log, one named owner and a written callback clock. Outsourced answering costs real money and has no proven conversion lift.
Lazur can point at settings, guide you through them and draft callbacks. It does not answer your phone.

blocks.text: What the research says about law firm missed calls

Most of the hard evidence comes from one secret-shopper study. Clio's 2024 Legal Trends work sent test contacts to 500 US law firms. The 2Civility summary of that work says the share of firms that answered a prospective client's phone call fell from 56% in 2019 to 40% in 2024. Email responses fell too, from 40% to 33%.

The harder number is 48%. That share of firms neither answered the phone nor called the prospect back. A missed call is one problem. A missed call with no callback is the real loss, and it is the part you can control.

blocks.title: Read the primary source
blocks.text: Clio's own report page was not reachable when this page was researched. The figures here come from 2Civility's summary of it. Pull the primary report before you quote these numbers to a partner or a client.
Why the 35% figure needs a careful read

A 2025 press release from Law Leaders reports a different picture. It says 35% of 1,200 calls to small and mid-sized US law firms went completely unanswered. The calls ran over four weeks, from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. local time, using public numbers and local caller IDs.

The release does not say how many firms were called. It describes Law Leaders as an Arizona-based ABS law firm and a legal AI technology company. Read the 35% as a warning sign, not a benchmark you can apply to your own firm.

The same release puts lost revenue at $109 billion a year. It does not explain how that figure was made. It cites a voicemail statistic only to unnamed national data. This page does not use either number.
Why response speed still matters

Older research points the same way. A 2011 Harvard Business Review article, The Short Life of Online Sales Leads, opens with a plain line. It says: 'Our research shows that most companies are not responding nearly fast enough.' I could only read that introduction, so this page does not quote its figures.
Treat that as a direction, not a measurement. Your firm can test its own speed with a simple log. A log tells you more about your intake than any industry average.
What a missed call costs a law firm
Most of the cost stays off the books. A missed call does not show up as a line item. It shows up as a consult that never got booked, and as a prospect who hired the firm that picked up.

Here is a worked example. A prospect calls at 4:40 p.m. on a Friday. Nobody answers. The voicemail says the office is closed and lists a general address. The prospect calls the next firm on the list before Monday morning, and your firm never hears about the matter.
You cannot know whether that prospect had a case you would have taken. That blind spot is the real cost. The fix starts with a log, not a guess.
Measure your law firm intake phone calls in one week

Run a simple test before you change anything. Call your main number three times on a weekday, from a phone whose number is not saved in your contacts. Call at 9:00 a.m., 12:30 p.m. and 5:30 p.m. Log each call in a table like this one.

blocks.caption: Blank test log. Fill it in during the week.

blocks.text: Repeat the test for two weeks. Count the answers. Note which times fail. If the 12:30 p.m. call goes unanswered every time, your lunch coverage is the problem, not your greeting. Fix the gap that repeats.
Use a number a prospect would not recognize. A saved contact can behave differently when screening is on, so your own phone may not show what a stranger sees.
Set up Calls from iPhone and Screen Unknown Callers on Mac
Start with the requirements. Apple's guides list conditions that trip people up. Check each one before you blame the software or the phone line.

items: Use the same Apple Account on your iPhone and Mac, on the same Wi-Fi network.
On iPhone, confirm iOS 8.1 or later and an activated carrier plan. On iOS 18 or later, go to Settings > Apps > Phone > Calls on Other Devices.
On the Mac, open FaceTime > Settings and make sure Calls from iPhone is selected.
On a Mac mini, Mac Studio or Mac Pro, connect an external microphone or headset. Apple says those models need one to make or receive calls.

blocks.text: For screening, use the Phone app on your Mac. It needs macOS Tahoe 26 or later. Choose Phone > Settings > Calls, then select Screen Unknown Callers. With screening on, the app answers unsaved numbers. It rings you only after the caller gives a name and a reason.

That is a trade. Screening cuts spam, but a prospect who will not give a reason never reaches you. Make two test calls from an unsaved number before you rely on it, then check the result against your log.
Mistakes that send prospects to voicemail

items: Using FaceTime's Silence Unknown Callers for intake. Apple says it sends calls to voicemail, which is a poor fit for a first call from a new prospect.
Forgetting a filter you turned on months ago. Check screening and silencing settings each time you change devices or accounts.
Writing a greeting that promises nothing. Say who you are and when someone will reply, but only promise what you can keep.
Making one person the only route for calls. When that person is in court, the phone rings out with nobody to take the message.
Ignoring calls after hours. Decide what after-hours callers get, then write it down where the team can see it.

blocks.text: What a law firm answering service costs, and what to check

Outsourced answering is the usual next step. Smith.ai's pricing page lists human-receptionist plans of $300 a month for 30 calls, $810 a month for 90 calls and $2,100 a month for 300 calls. Extra calls cost $11.50, $10.50 and $8.50 each. Twelve-month subscriptions get a 10% discount.

blocks.caption: Smith.ai list prices, as shown on its pricing page

blocks.text: The page shows a copyright year but no pricing date. Third-party guides quote different tiers, so confirm the current price with the vendor before you budget. Ask for a sample call summary too, so you can see what the attorney receives.

No controlled study I found shows that AI receptionists or answering services raise conversion. Vendor case studies exist, but they do not publish their methods. Score any service with the same call log you built this week, and compare the booked consults, not the call counts.
If a service takes calls about a matter, check your firm's rules on client data and confidentiality first. Follow your employer's rules, even when a vendor says its setup is secure.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It points at the setting you need and draws a circle and a label around it. For a multi-step setup, it guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.

It does not answer your phone. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It is not an add-in for any app, and it has no partnerships with app makers. A person or a service still has to answer the call.

For intake, the useful parts are the small ones. Hold fn to dictate a call note at the cursor in any app. Ask Lazur to draft a callback email, then read it and send it yourself. Research jobs run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension, and come back with a summary and a report.

Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

If your firm handles intake in Apple Mail or Outlook, see [AI assistant for Apple Mail](/apps/apple-mail) and [Outlook for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/outlook). Those pages cover the screens in more detail.
Edge cases: after hours, several offices and mixed practice areas

Some firms need more than one rule. If you run two offices on one number, the greeting may need to name both, or route calls by office. If you take intake for several practice areas, one script will not fit every call. Sort by practice area first, then send each type to the right person.

Calls after hours need their own rule. Decide now whether a call that comes in at 5:00 p.m. on a Friday gets a callback that day, or the next business morning. Put the rule in the greeting only if the team can keep it. A broken promise costs more than a plain message.

Court days break most plans. When the owner is in court, the backup needs a short list. It should say which calls can wait, which need a same-day reply, and who to tell. Keep that list on one page where the backup can find it in seconds.
What to do after you take the call

A good call can still get lost. Write the note within a minute of hanging up. Include the caller's name, the one-line reason for the call, the callback number and the time you promised to reply. A note with those four items lets anyone on the team act.
Keep one shared list for open intakes, not a sticky note or a personal inbox. Review it each morning. Mark each item called back, booked or closed. The list costs nothing, and it works on any Mac.
Change one thing at a time

Pick one change, test it for two weeks, then decide. Changing five things at once hides which one worked. Start with the owner and the callback clock, since both cost nothing to try, and then look at screening.

faq.question: Do most law firms miss prospective client calls?
faq.answer: The best data I found is a 2024 secret-shopper study of 500 US firms. It found 40% answered a prospect's call, down from 56% in 2019. A 2025 vendor release reports 35% of its test calls went unanswered. Neither study measures your firm, so run your own two-week log.

faq.question: Is the $109 billion lost revenue figure real?
faq.answer: I could not verify it. The Law Leaders release gives the number but does not explain how it was calculated. Do not quote it to a partner or a client without the method behind it.

faq.question: Does Screen Unknown Callers block new clients?
faq.answer: It can. With screening on, the Phone app answers unsaved numbers and rings you only after the caller gives a name and a reason. A caller who will not give a reason may never reach you. Test it before you rely on it.

faq.question: Can I use FaceTime's Silence Unknown Callers for intake?
faq.answer: Usually not. Apple says it silences unknown callers and sends them to voicemail. A new prospect who reaches voicemail may not leave a message. Use Phone screening for intake instead, and check the result in your log.

faq.question: Do Mac mini and Mac Studio need a microphone for calls?
faq.answer: Yes, according to Apple. Mac mini, Mac Studio and Mac Pro need an external microphone or headset to make or receive calls. Plug one in before you test Calls from iPhone.

faq.question: Are AI receptionists proven to win more clients?
faq.answer: No controlled study I found shows that. Vendor case studies exist, but they do not publish their methods. Test any service with your own call log before you commit money to it.

faq.question: What do I need for Calls from iPhone on my Mac?
faq.answer: Your iPhone needs iOS 8.1 or later and an activated carrier plan. Both devices need the same Apple Account and the same Wi-Fi network. On the Mac, open FaceTime > Settings and select Calls from iPhone.

faq.question: Can Lazur answer my phone for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant on the Mac. It can point at settings, guide you through steps, draft text and dictate notes. It does not answer calls or click buttons for you.

faq.question: Is client information safe if I use Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Follow your firm's rules on client data before you use any tool with matter details.

costs.title: The matter you never hear about
costs.text: A missed call is invisible in your books. The prospect simply goes elsewhere, and nobody on your team learns why. You cannot see the matter that never came in, so measure your answer rate and booked consults to size the loss.

costs.title: Staff time spent chasing
costs.text: Every missed call turns into a callback, an email and a note later. Those steps take time from people who already have a full day. Count how many calls your team returns each week, and how many minutes each one takes.

costs.title: First impression with a new client
costs.text: The first contact often sets the tone. A ring that goes unanswered, followed by a vague voicemail, tells the caller something about your firm. The 2024 secret-shopper study found drops in both phone and email responses.

costs.title: Answering service fees
costs.text: An outside answering service turns a staffing problem into a monthly bill. On Smith.ai's pricing page, a plan with 30 included calls costs $300 a month, and each extra call adds $11.50. Compare that bill with the consults you expect to book.

causes.title: Nobody owns the phone
causes.text: Calls rarely have a single owner. The receptionist assumes the attorney will call back. The attorney assumes the front desk handles intake. Each call falls between two people, so it sits. Name one owner for intake, with a named backup for lunch, leave and court days.

causes.title: Calls land in the busy windows
causes.text: Most phone trouble lands in the same few hours. A lawyer is in court, a paralegal is on a deadline, or a receptionist is covering three lines at once. Calls in those windows go to voicemail or ring out. Check your log to find the hours when you miss the most.

causes.title: Voicemail is the last stop
causes.text: A prospect who reaches a generic voicemail has no reason to wait. The greeting says nothing about who you are or when someone will reply. The caller can dial the next firm on the list, and nothing in your greeting gave them a reason to stay.

causes.title: Filters hide new numbers
causes.text: Screening and silencing settings help against spam. They also hide a first-time prospect who has never called before. Apple's Phone app asks unknown callers for a name and a reason. A prospect who will not do that may never reach anyone at the firm.

causes.title: No callback clock
causes.text: When a call is returned, there is often no deadline. The note sits in a shared inbox, a personal email or a sticky note. Without a clock, follow-up slides to next week, and the prospect has already called someone else.

causes.title: Small teams and thin coverage
causes.text: A small firm may have one receptionist, one paralegal and a lawyer who handles intake between court dates. When one person is out, calls pile up. A 2016 study of 12,825 licensed attorneys found 28% reported mild or higher depression. It did not measure phone handling, so read it as context, not proof.

fixes.title: Name one owner and one backup
fixes.text: Put one name on intake in writing, and add a backup for lunch, court days and leave. Tell the backup what to do with each type of call. Review the owner list each quarter, and again whenever someone leaves the firm.

fixes.title: Write a callback clock
fixes.text: Pick a deadline your team can keep, such as the same business day for calls before 2:00 p.m. and the next morning for later calls. Put that promise in the voicemail greeting. Track each open call in a shared list, not on a sticky note.

fixes.title: Use a short intake script
fixes.text: Ask for the caller's name, a callback number and a one-line reason for calling. Keep the script short, since the first call does not need the full story. A consistent script keeps the notes usable for the attorney who reads them later.

fixes.title: Decide what screening does to new prospects
fixes.text: Screening cuts spam, but it also hides first-time callers who will not give a reason. Pick the setting after a two-week test. If you lose real prospects, turn screening off during business hours, when someone can answer the phone.

fixes.title: Review missed calls every Friday
fixes.text: Each Friday, read the week's missed-call list. Mark each call as called back, booked or lost. Look for a pattern in the day and time. A pattern tells you which fix to try next, so you do not change everything at once.

fixes.title: Put after-hours rules in writing
fixes.text: Decide whether after-hours calls get a callback by the next business morning. Write the promise down and keep it. If the team cannot keep a promise, do not make it in the greeting, because a broken promise is worse than a plain message.

fixes.title: Dictate or type a note within a minute
fixes.text: Right after the call, write the name, the reason, the callback time and the number. Any dictation tool or a typed note works. Paste the note into your intake form or matter file. Follow your firm's rules on client data when you do.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Baseline your answer rate
plan.text: Run the three test calls from the measurement section, at 9:00 a.m., 12:30 p.m. and 5:30 p.m. Log who answered, how long the wait was and what the voicemail said.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Name the owner and the backup
plan.text: Write one name for intake and one backup. Send the note to both. Include what to do with calls during court days, lunch and leave.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Write the callback clock
plan.text: Pick the deadline for same-day and next-morning callbacks. Put it in the voicemail greeting and at the top of your shared list. Keep it simple enough for anyone on the team to follow.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Test screening on your Mac
plan.text: Turn on Screen Unknown Callers in Phone > Settings > Calls. Call from an unsaved number twice. Note whether the call rang through after the caller gave a name and a reason.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review and decide
plan.text: Read the week's missed-call list. Mark each call as called back, booked or lost. Decide whether to keep screening on, change the greeting, or price an answering service against the consults it books.
